title: Most stories are lies
translation: Most of the stories people pass around are lies. Maybe the truth is just too dull. People make things bigger than they were to begin with. Add a few years and some distance, and they tell it however they like. Once somebody writes it down, that's the version that sticks.

Take the amazing things the best people in some art are supposed to have done. People who don't know the field talk about them as if they were gods. People who do know it don't believe a word. Things you only hear about are always different when you see them.

Someone who rattles off whatever comes into his head, without caring that he's being found out as he speaks, is soon seen through. Then there's the man who doesn't really believe it himself but passes it on just as he heard it, his nose twitching with pride. It isn't his lie. The frightening kind is the lie told very convincingly, a little vague here and there, as if the teller isn't quite sure, but with every detail fitting.

A lie that makes you look good, you don't argue with much. And a lie everyone is enjoying? There's no point being the one person to say "That's not how it was." So you sit there listening, and before you know it you've been made a witness, and the story is more fixed than ever.

Either way, the world is full of lies. Assume things are ordinary and nothing special, and you won't go wrong. The stories common people tell are all about astonishing things. Well-bred people don't tell strange stories.

That said, the miracles of the Buddhas and the gods, and the lives of the saints, aren't something to dismiss outright. Swallowing them whole, the way people swallow gossip, is silly. But saying "Never happened" gets you nowhere either. So, mostly, treat them as if they were true. Don't believe them completely, but don't doubt them and make fun of them either.

literal: Things that are told and passed on in the world: perhaps because the truth is uninteresting, most of them are all lies.

People tell things as more than they are, and all the more when years and months have passed and places are far apart, they tell it as they like, and when it is also written down with the brush, it soon becomes fixed.

Things like the splendid feats of masters in the various arts: ignorant people who do not know that art talk of them recklessly as if (the masters were) gods, but people who know the art do not believe it at all.
What one hears by report and what one sees: in everything, they differ.
Those who scatter words as their mouths lead them, not caring that (the lie) is being exposed even as they speak, are soon heard as (telling) groundless things.
Also, one who, though he himself thinks it is not true, tells it just as someone told it, twitching around his nose, is not (telling) his own lie.
A lie told plausibly, here and there feigning vagueness, pretending not to know well, and yet fitting the details together: that is a frightening thing.
A lie told so as to bring honour to oneself, people do not dispute much;
a lie that everyone enjoys: since it is pointless for one person to say 'it was not so', while one sits listening, one is even made into a witness, and it surely becomes all the more fixed.
In any case, it is a world with many lies.
If one just understands things as the usual, unremarkable things they are, one will not go wrong in anything.
The stories of lower people contain only things that astonish the ear.
Good people do not tell strange things.
Though I say this, the miracles of Buddhas and gods, and the lives of avatars, should not be entirely disbelieved.

In this (case), just as it is foolish to believe worldly lies earnestly, it is also pointless to say things like 'surely not', so generally one should deal with them as true, not believe them wholeheartedly, and also not doubt and mock them.

notes.text: あいなし: 'dull, not interesting'. にや: 'is it perhaps that…?', with the rest (あらむ) left out. Kenkō offers it as a guess.
{虚言|そらごと}: 'empty words', a lie. The word runs through the whole section.
{境|さかひ}: here 'place, region'. Distance in time and distance in space both help a story grow.
かたくな: 'narrow, ignorant, without taste'. Compare {頑|かたくな}なる{人|ひと} in section 137.

notes.quote: 音にきくと見る時とは
notes.text: {音|おと}: here 'rumour, report'. {音|おと}に{聞|き}く: 'to know only by hearsay'. Modern Japanese still says {音|おと}に{聞|き}こえた 'famous'.
ごめく: 'to twitch, to wriggle'. The twitching nose is usually explained as pride at having a story to tell.
おぼめく: 'to act unsure, to be vague'. The skilled liar is vague on purpose, which is what makes the rest believable. つまづま: 'the ends, the details'.
さへ: 'even'. You kept quiet, so now you count as someone who was there and can confirm it.
{権者|ごんじや}: a Buddha or bodhisattva who appears in this world in human form ({権|ごん}: 'temporary, provisional'). Their lives were told as stories of saints and wonders.
あひしらふ: 'to deal with, to respond to'. The advice is a middle way: go along politely, without full belief and without mockery.
